topics.title: FiberSurvivors: a browser survivors-like for Fiber

recent_posts.topic_title: FiberSurvivors: a browser survivors-like for Fiber
recent_posts.author: TranNhi27
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi everyone!
I’ve been working on FiberSurvivors, a top-down survivors-like (kinda like Vampire Survivors) that runs in the browser, where the CKB you earn and the upgrade cards you buy are all paid over Fiber.
So a run goes like this:
You open the game and a Fiber node starts in your browser, with its own wallet
You fund it from the testnet faucet
Press Play, and the game opens a channel to the hub node (game’s reward liquidity)
Clear a level, and the hub pays you CKB
Buy upgrade cards mid-run by paying an invoice
Cash out at the end, the channel closes and your CKB goes back on-chain
All you need is a browser tab, no extension, no local node, no CLI. Everything runs on testnet.
The Loop Graph:
fund a channel ──► fight through 10 levels ──► hub pays each level cleared
▲ │
│ ▼
stronger build ◄──── spend earnings on upgrade cards
│
▼
cash out ──► channel closes, CKB settles on-chain
So it’s more rewards vs more power. You earn more if you buy fewer cards, kite well and win, but if you lose a level, the run ends there. Right now there are 10 levels with a dragon boss at the end, more might come later.
Motivation
While learning Fiber and CKB, I felt like Fiber fits PvP games best, since two players can pay each other directly over a channel, so you don’t have to put all the trust on one server. But for UX, I wanted players to have a smooth experience without setting up a local node or finding someone to match with, and on a testnet demo it’s pretty hard to find another player online. So in the end it became a single-player game where you earn CKB by playing and spend it on upgrades, at least for now.
image735×1287 126 KB
image746×1293 167 KB
image748×1302 170 KB
image807×1280 113 KB
Try it
Demo: https://zesty-youtiao-8586ae.netlify.app
SDK repo: Fiber WebGL SDK
The game source isn’t public since it uses some paid assets (Feel and the Vefects Effect Pack), and their licenses don’t allow sharing them. But all the Fiber parts are in the SDK, which is fully open.
How it works
The game is built in Unity (WebGL). For the Fiber part I use my own Fiber WebGL SDK, which runs Fiber’s WASM node (@nervosnetwork/fiber-js) inside the build.
On the other side there’s one fnn node (the hub) on a small cloud VM, plus a small Express server next to it. Every player opens one channel to the hub, and all rewards and card payments go through it.
The server is the one deciding money, not the client:
Rewards: The coins you pick up only count once you reach the exit. That’s when the client claims them, the server checks the claim, and the hub pays you. Die before the exit and those coins are gone. The full campaign is 10 levels and pays up to 216 CKB
Cards: When you buy a card, the client only sends the card id. The server makes an invoice with the price, then the client decodes it and checks the price matches what it showed you before paying. Cards are 5 to 45 CKB, so if you buy a lot you can actually end a run with less than you started with lol
Cash out: Cash out closes the channel and settles both sides on-chain
Each player channel is 400 CKB, and the hub puts in 400 CKB on its side too.
The SDK
While building this I ended up turning all the Fiber stuff into a Unity package, which I submitted to the Gone in 60ms Hackathon where my winning chances were also gone in 60ms
Anyway, any Unity WebGL game can use it too:
IPaymentGateway: start the node, connect, open/close channels, keysend
IInvoicePaymentGateway: decode an invoice, check the amount, pay
IUdtPaymentGateway: xUDT channels and payments, route dry-runs
IFiberWallet: on-chain CKB balance
IFiberDiagnostics: peers and channels
There’s a sample scene in the repo if you want to try it without the game.
Limitations
Well, to be honest this is a tech demo for “a Fiber node inside a Unity browser game”. The money side is protected: the client never decides an amount, rewards come from the server, and card prices come in server-made invoices. But the gameplay itself isn’t verified
You trust the server: The server can’t see the gameplay itself, but it rejects claims that are out of order, too fast, or have more coins than the level could drop. With one claim per level per session and a payout cap per player, that’s what stops reward spamming for now, but there’s no real anti-cheat.
The key lives in the browser: Like any Fiber node, it signs automatically, but here the key is kept in the browser’s localStorage for this site. If you clear your site data, the key and any CKB in it are gone. That’s okay for testnet, but letting players back up the key, or binding it to their own CKB wallet, would fix this.
Opening a channel takes a few minutes on testnet since it waits for on-chain confirmation.
How to play
There’s a tutorial in the game, but here are the controls:
Controls: WASD to move, attacks are automatic, 1 to 4 to use a skill, left-click to aim, right-click to cancel.
Some tips
If the channel open fails, wait a minute and try again, testnet can be slow sometimes
Don’t forget to cash out at the end to get your CKB back on-chain
Credits
Kudos to these free assets, they helped me build this a lot faster:
KayKit’s Packs for my game including Characters, Skeleton Enemies, Environment, Animations
My cute Dragon Boss
Space Game GUI Kit
500 Free Skill Icons
Thank you for reading till here, any feedback is welcome

  • You trust the server: The server can’t see the gameplay itself, but it rejects claims that are out of order, too fast, or have more coins than the level could drop. topics.title: Spark Program Proposal: Corven cloud-native IDE

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program Proposal: Corven cloud-native IDE
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @lestonEth,
Thank you for your continued interest in the Spark Program and for submitting the Corven cloud-native IDE proposal.
After review by the Spark Program committee, your proposal has been assigned a status of Pending. This is not a rejection, but an invitation to revise and resubmit.
The committee acknowledges the value of your work — a browser-based IDE that lowers the barrier for new developers to build on CKB is genuinely useful, and the progress you’ve made on the CKB foundation (workspace management, devnet provisioning, contract templates, transaction debugger) is impressive.
Main Revision Recommendations:
Deliverables clarification: Please explicitly state what the expected deliverables and outputs of this phase are. The committee needs a clear, measurable list of what will be produced by the end of the 4-week period.
Website accessibility: The committee was unable to access the provided website (corvan.space). This raises concerns about whether the project is actually operational and can support the proposed activities. Please confirm the website’s status and provide a working link, or explain the current situation.
Acceptance criteria: The committee would like to be clear upfront that if the final report, test data, and community feedback do not meet the committee’s requirements, the project will not be approved for completion. Please ensure your proposal includes concrete — and verifiable — plans for how you will collect and present this evidence.
Testing plan: Since this phase includes hands-on testing with Web3 developer clubs in Kenya, please clarify how the sessions will be conducted and what specific feedback you plan to collect from participants.
Regarding the website being down — if there are hosting issues or recent changes, please let us know. Please revise and resubmit based on the feedback above. We will arrange a new round of review as soon as possible.
Best regards,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

topics.title: Spark Program | LiquidLane: Fiber Receive Capacity Marketplace | RESUBMISSION

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | LiquidLane: Fiber Receive Capacity Marketplace | RESUBMISSION
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @Fidelcoder,
Thank you for taking the time to revise and resubmit the LiquidLane proposal based on our earlier feedback. The committee has completed its review and, after careful discussion, regrets to reject the LiquidLane project at this time.
We want to be transparent about the reasoning behind this decision:
1. **Security considerations were not adequately addressed**: As an infrastructure project handling channel funding and fee distribution, the proposal does not sufficiently address the security model — including fund custody, withdrawal paths, and what happens in the event of node downtime or malicious behavior from either party. The committee believes these risks should have been identified and mitigated at the design stage.
2. **Technical implementation remains premature**: The current implementation shows signs of incompleteness — interfaces are not fully connected, and the wallet connector relies solely on JoyID without leveraging CCC (CKBers’ Codebase), which is the recommended SDK and provides a unified wallet connection layer. Given that CKB already has well-established tooling in this area, the committee expects new projects to build on the existing stack rather than reinventing or bypassing it.
3. **Lack of demonstrated long-term operational commitment**: This is an infrastructure-level project, and the committee did not see evidence of a sustainable plan for ongoing maintenance, node coordination, and user support after the initial grant period. Infrastructure projects require continuous upkeep to remain viable, and the proposal does not adequately address this.
We appreciate the work your team has put into LiquidLane and acknowledge the effort behind the resubmission. However, the committee suggests that rather than targeting bottom-layer infrastructure — which demands significant experience and long-term commitment — you consider pivoting toward **application-layer development**. There is meaningful value to be created by building user-facing payment experiences, merchant tools, or wallets that integrate with existing infrastructure such as Fiber Network, rather than attempting to build the infrastructure itself.
If in the future you plan to develop a more scoped, application-focused project with a clear security model and demonstrated technical readiness, we would welcome a new application.
Thank you very much for all the hard work your team has put in. Keep building, and feel free to reach out anytime!
Best,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @Mulandi_Cecilia:
Thank you for sharing with the committee your interactions with other developers in the community about zk-Lock.
The committee would like to align with you on two priorities for community engagement:
Engaging non-developers in the community: The committee is glad to see you interacting with other developers in the community. However, when we suggested strengthening community engagement, we especially hoped you would explain to community members without a technical background—not just developers—what use cases zk-Lock enables, how they can use it, and what tangible outcomes they can achieve with it. We believe broader community outreach is essential for this foundational component to become fully integrated into the ecosystem.
Interactive frontend: The committee would like to see an interactive frontend that integrates the SDK and contracts, even if its functionality is very simple. The goal is to let community members with no development experience participate in the project and try it out firsthand. This would also demonstrate the project’s value proposition in a clear, tangible way and help the community understand what zk-Lock can do beyond its technical specifications.
We are not currently asking you to deliver a polished, production-ready product; a basic interface demonstrating the core functionality will suffice. If you need help implementing the frontend or would like to discuss how to build a community demo, please feel free to reach out. The committee would be happy to support you. We would also be glad to connect you with other grant recipients who have built similar interactive demos for reference.
Best regards,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee
cc: @zz_tovarishch , @yixiu.ckbfans.bit , @Hanssen

topics.title: [DIS] FiberLatch Access - Open-Source Access Control for Fiber Payments

recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] FiberLatch Access - Open-Source Access Control for Fiber Payments
recent_posts.author: Ticoworld
recent_posts.content_text:
Post-grant update: FiberFlow integration and real Fiber testnet settlement
Hi everyone,
I’ve continued working on FiberLatch after the grant, mostly by testing where it can actually fit into existing Fiber applications.
One of the projects I tried was FiberFlow.
The integration worked around a simple boundary:
Fiber payment → FiberFlow invoice.paid → FiberLatch access → protected resource
FiberFlow handles the payment. Once the application trusts the paid event, FiberLatch handles the access that comes after it.
While testing this, I noticed I was repeating the same PostgreSQL logic in both the FiberFlow integration and a separate FiberLatch reference app, especially around limited-use receipts and safe concurrent redemption.
So I extracted that part into a small optional package:
@fiberlatch/postgres-store@0.1.0
The main @fiberlatch/access package is still 0.1.1.
Real settlement test
The first FiberFlow integration was tested around the webhook flow, but I still wanted to complete it with a real Fiber payment.
Since the hosted FiberFlow service was unavailable, I ran FiberFlow locally on testnet and tested the whole flow with separate payer and merchant Fiber nodes.
The payment settled successfully.
From the same payment:
FiberFlow moved the invoice to Paid
the real signed invoice.paid webhook reached the store
FiberLatch created one entitlement
the purchaser retrieved the signed receipt
uses 1, 2 and 3 succeeded
use 4 was denied
the final redemption count stayed at 3/3
The first webhook delivery also timed out after it had already been processed, so FiberFlow retried it. The retry still left only one FiberLatch entitlement, which was a useful idempotency check.
I also checked that another account could not retrieve or use the purchaser’s access.
What I learned from this
This test made the FiberLatch boundary clearer.
FiberLatch is not trying to replace Fiber payment tooling. The application still decides whether a payment or permission is valid.
FiberLatch starts after that decision and turns it into a signed access receipt with things like subject binding, resource scope and limited uses.
The PostgreSQL package is just an optional reusable store for apps already using PostgreSQL.
This is currently tested in my FiberFlow fork and local setup, so this is not upstream FiberFlow adoption yet.
It was also testnet-only, so I’m not making any mainnet or production-readiness claim from this test.
Full settlement evidence:
github.com/Ticoworld/fiberflow
use-published-fiberlatch-postgres-store/examples/store/FIBER_SETTLEMENT_ACCEPTANCE.md
chore
# Real Fiber testnet settlement acceptance
Date: October 10, 2026 (Africa/Lagos).
Branch: `chore/use-published-fiberlatch-postgres-store`.
Source commit: `2f4b28f5ff40e087580a7bc9dd619f0a2bed5e06`.
This proves a real Fiber TESTNET settlement through locally self-hosted FiberFlow
triggering the existing FiberLatch access integration. This report records the
completed local acceptance run.

Post-grant update: FiberFlow integration and real Fiber testnet settlement

Hi everyone,

I’ve continued working on FiberLatch after the grant, mostly by testing where it can actually fit into existing Fiber applications.

One of the projects I tried was FiberFlow.

The integration worked around a simple boundary:

Fiber payment → FiberFlow invoice.paid → FiberLatch access → protected resource

FiberFlow handles the payment. Once the application trusts the paid event, FiberLatch handles the access that comes after it.

While testing this, I noticed I was repeating the same PostgreSQL logic in both the FiberFlow integration and a separate FiberLatch reference app, especially around limited-use receipts and safe concurrent redemption.

So I extracted that part into a small optional package:

@fiberlatch/postgres-store@0.1.0

The main @fiberlatch/access package is still 0.1.1.

Real settlement test

The first FiberFlow integration was tested around the webhook flow, but I still wanted to complete it with a real Fiber payment.

Since the hosted FiberFlow service was unavailable, I ran FiberFlow locally on testnet and tested the whole flow with separate payer and merchant Fiber nodes.

The payment settled successfully.

From the same payment:

  • FiberFlow moved the invoice to Paid
  • the real signed invoice.paid webhook reached the store
  • FiberLatch created one entitlement
  • the purchaser retrieved the signed receipt
  • uses 1, 2 and 3 succeeded
  • use 4 was denied
  • the final redemption count stayed at 3/3

The first webhook delivery also timed out after it had already been processed, so FiberFlow retried it. The retry still left only one FiberLatch entitlement, which was a useful idempotency check.

I also checked that another account could not retrieve or use the purchaser’s access.

What I learned from this

This test made the FiberLatch boundary clearer.

FiberLatch is not trying to replace Fiber payment tooling. The application still decides whether a payment or permission is valid.

FiberLatch starts after that decision and turns it into a signed access receipt with things like subject binding, resource scope and limited uses.

The PostgreSQL package is just an optional reusable store for apps already using PostgreSQL.

This is currently tested in my FiberFlow fork and local setup, so this is not upstream FiberFlow adoption yet.

It was also testnet-only, so I’m not making any mainnet or production-readiness claim from this test.

Full settlement evidence:

Thanks for reaching out, Salman. I’d like to support you this, but I’d want two things explicitly covered in the hardening milestones.
From the current code, the issuer appears able to spend the collateral without consuming the loan cell, bypassing the loan’s release checks. The borrow/repay checks also count output balances rather than net funds received.
Could you include enforcing the loan rules on every collateral spend, and verifying actual net disbursement and repayment, with tests covering both?

topics.title: CKB Pulse: who is building on CKB, live

recent_posts.topic_title: CKB Pulse: who is building on CKB, live
recent_posts.author: T_Silva
recent_posts.content_text:
CKB Pulse: who is building on CKB, live
Hi everyone,
We made CKB Pulse, a page that shows the public work on CKB as it happens on GitHub.
CKB Pulse
CKB Pulse · Last 7 days
627 updates by 62 people in 58 projects, in the last 7 days.
Every project is a block. When someone pushes code, proposes or reviews a change, reports a problem or publishes a release, a light flies from their face to the project and the block grows. Watch it live, or replay the last 24 hours or the last 7 days in a minute or two. Drag to turn the view, tap a block to open the project.
It is written for people who never open GitHub too: plain words, in English, 中文 and Português.
What you can see
Highlights of the day, the week and the month: the most active projects, people and organisations, with medals.
Active developers per month over the last two years, and how many committed for the first time.
New CKB projects from the last 14 days, flagged when they appear. Follow projects and people on your device and get a notice when they move.
For projects with contracts on mainnet: the CKB in cells that use them, transactions and last use, from the CKB explorer and the ckb-cli deployment files the project commits.
A picture to share for the highlights, any project or any person.
The counters at the top open everything as plain lists, for keyboards and screen readers.
How it finds projects
Nobody keeps the list by hand. Every few hours it searches GitHub for repositories that use CKB libraries (CCC, Lumos, Spore, RGB++, JoyID, ckb-std, the Go and Java SDKs and more) or carry CKB topics. It also checks the other projects of the people working in them, and the repositories behind scripts registered on the CKB explorer. A new organisation appears on its own when it starts working, and leaves after 30 days without work by people.
Missing a project? Add a topic such as ckb or nervos to its repository, or type the GitHub name in the “New” tab, under “Missing someone?”. It joins when GitHub shows public CKB work from the last 30 days.
How it counts
Only work by people. Bots, AI agents working on their own branches (claude/, codex/, copilot/ and others) and the same update pushed day after day by a script show as grey sparks and stay out of the numbers and medals. Merging an agent’s work still counts. For medals, one person counts at most 10 updates per project per hour.
GitHub’s public events arrive 30 seconds to a few hours late, so live means as soon as GitHub tells us.
The code is open, MIT: GitHub - LusoCryptoLabs/ckb-pulse: Live GitHub activity of the CKB ecosystem, drawn in 3D · GitHub
What would you like to see on it, and who is missing?

recent_posts.author: phroi
recent_posts.content_text:
chenyukang:
requirement that at least one input must have the same lock used with the DAO cell
IMHO this fair: this protocol doesn’t require to re-deposit, it doesn’t use fancy tech and it tries to minimizes failure points. Kudos to @xjd!!
If it creates troubles for RGB++ users (or generally those whose lock change at every tx), then I would suggest these users to use a compatible wallet just for using this protocol.
If reusing a lock is a perceived security issue for Q-day, then Quantum Purse should give enough peace of mind.
chenyukang:
A large DAO holder, custodian, exchange, or colluding coalition may still create a permissionless Proposal paying itself and supply enough genuine voting power to satisfy every configured condition
This is one of the original problems I raised on DAO v1.1 and I can’t see a clean solution.
Independently from reviewed projects, my feeling is that voting with money is short-sighted for the very reasons we both pointed out: it works until it doesn’t…
I would personally try to see how a CKBA-based system could work rather than risking hostile takeovers from wealthy CKB holders.
chenyukang:
Generally, how do you think about this solution?
All in all, promising and well put togheter, non sure I would deploy it. For the usual technical issues, I’ll keep using Github.
Phroi
PS: a few years ago Vitalik analyzed Decentralized Governance and … it’s messy: Moving beyond coin voting governance
